\chapter{Hablado, Comido, Vivido --- The Participle}
\label{ch:participle}
\hlchaptermodality{102}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can form the participle of any regular verb, and know it never changes for person.}

Complete ES-C49-participio: form the three participles and say whether the form changes with the speaker.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablado / comido / vivido]{hablado, comido, vivido — the participle}

\label{lesson:ES-C49-participio}



\begin{quote}
Your three verb families, once more: \emph{hablar}, \emph{comer}, \emph{vivir}. This chapter gives each of them one new form, and two of the three get the same one.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two endings, not three}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{habl}ar $\to$ \textbf{hablado} · \textbf{com}er $\to$ \textbf{comido} · \textbf{viv}ir $\to$ \textbf{vivido}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{-ar} verbs take \textbf{-ado}.
  \item \textbf{-er} and \textbf{-ir} verbs both take \textbf{-ido}.
\end{itemize}

You have seen those two families collapse into one before: in the preterite, where \emph{comí} and \emph{viví} have identical endings. It happens here for the same reason it happened there — the difference between \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} was never deep, and outside the present tense it mostly stops existing.

So this is one new ending and one you can predict.

The word itself does not change for who is speaking. \emph{Hablado} is \emph{hablado} whether you, I, or a hundred people did the speaking. That is unusual enough to notice: every other verb form you hold has been carrying a person on its back.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Grammarians call this a \textbf{participle}, from Latin \textbf{participium} — \textquotedblleft{}the form that \textbf{takes part}.\textquotedblright{} It was named for doing two jobs at once: it is built from a verb, and it behaves like an adjective.

You can see the adjective half immediately. \emph{Cansado} (\textquotedblleft{}tired\textquotedblright{}) is the participle of \emph{cansar}, and it agrees like any adjective: \emph{cansada}, \emph{cansados}. The same shape, doing adjective work.

Next chapter puts it to its verb work instead — and there, held in place by another word, it stops agreeing with anything at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablado, comido, vivido\textquotedblright{} — one ending, then the shared one
  \item \textquotedblleft{}comí, viví\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}comido, vivido\textquotedblright{} — the same merger, twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Participle of \emph{hablar}? (\emph{\textbf{Hablado}}.) Of \emph{comer} and \emph{vivir}? (\emph{\textbf{Comido}}, \emph{\textbf{vivido}} — the same ending.) What does \emph{participium} mean? (The form that \textbf{takes part} — verb and adjective at once.) Next: the word that turns it into a tense.
\end{tcolorbox}
